title: The Girl Made of Questions
summary: In the town of Certain, asking questions is forbidden — the townsfolk trade every 'why' to a hidden thing in exchange for a life without doubt. Ivo can't stop asking, and following her questions down into the dark, she finds out what the town has been feeding, and why.

chapters.title: The Town of Certain
chapters.body:
In the town of Certain, no one ever asked why.

It was the town's proudest quality. The people of Certain were, well, certain — about everything. They knew exactly how things were done, and they did them that way, and they never wondered whether they might be done differently, because wondering was not done. There was a deep, restful calm to the place. No one argued, because no one doubted. No one lay awake at night turning a question over, because no one had questions. Life in Certain was smooth and untroubled as a pond with no wind, and the townsfolk pitied the anxious, questioning people of other towns, who were forever unsure, forever asking, forever awake.

Ivo was nine, and she was a problem, because Ivo could not stop asking why.

It bubbled up out of her all the time. Why is the sky blue and not green? Why do we always eat supper at the sixth bell? Why is the north gate never opened? Why does everyone go quiet when I ask a question? The questions came to her the way breath comes — without her choosing them, simply because she was alive and awake and looking at the world. And every time she asked one, the grown-ups of Certain flinched, as if she'd said something shameful, and hushed her, and looked around nervously to see who had heard.

"We don't ask why, Ivo," her mother told her, over and over, with a fear in her voice the girl didn't understand. "It isn't done. Please. Please stop asking. For your own good. Before they notice."

"Before who notices?" Ivo asked — because of course she did.

And her mother went pale, and would not answer, and that non-answer was the biggest question of all.

Ivo began to watch. And watching — which is a kind of asking, done with the eyes — she noticed strange things. She noticed that on the night of each new moon, one grown-up of Certain would rise in the dark and walk, alone and glassy-eyed, to the old dry well at the center of town, and lean over it, and whisper something down into the black — and come back up the street lighter, calmer, emptier, and never speak of it. She noticed that these were always the grown-ups who had seemed, lately, a little troubled. A little uncertain. As if some doubt had crept into their smooth calm — and they had gone to the well to get rid of it.

And Ivo, who could not stop asking, asked herself the most dangerous question in Certain: what lives in the well, and what is the town feeding it?

So on the next new moon, instead of sleeping, Ivo followed.

chapters.title: What Lives in the Well
chapters.body:
Ivo followed a glassy-eyed baker to the dry well in the dark, and hid behind the stone rim, and watched him lean over the black mouth and whisper into it.

"I've been having doubts," the baker murmured down into the dark, in a flat, drained voice. "I wondered why we've always done things this way. I wondered if the north gate should be opened. I wondered... I wondered a great many things. Take them. Please. Take the wondering. Let me be certain again."

And something down in the well answered.

It was not a voice exactly — more a sound like dry pages turning, like wind through an empty house, rising up out of the black. And as it sounded, Ivo saw a pale mist come up out of the well and wind around the baker, and draw something out of him — she could see it leaving, faint wisps of light pulled from his head like thread from a spool — and the baker sighed, a long empty sigh, and straightened, and his eyes went smooth and calm and certain again, and he walked back home without a backward glance.

And from the well came a sound that Ivo, with a chill, recognized as satisfaction. A full, fed sound. The sound of a thing that had just eaten.

Ivo leaned over the rim and looked down into the dark, and asked — because she could not help it, because it was what she was made of — the question aloud: "What are you?"

The dry-pages sound rose up, and this time it made words, cold and old and pleased. "I am the Doubt-Eater," it said. "And this town has fed me for a hundred years, and grown fat and calm on the bargain. Long ago, the people of Certain were like people anywhere — full of questions, full of doubt, forever unsure, forever awake at night wondering if they were doing right. And it troubled them. So they found me. And we struck a bargain. They feed me their questions — every why, every doubt, every wondering — and in exchange I give them certainty. Peace. The smooth calm you see. Whenever a doubt troubles one of them, they bring it to me, and I eat it, and they are certain again." The sound curled with pleasure. "It is a fine bargain. For me. Because a question, little girl, is the most nourishing thing there is. And a town that has agreed to stop asking them is a feast that never ends."

"But why is it bad?" Ivo asked — and then, because she was Ivo, she kept going, the questions tumbling out. "If they're happy? If they're calm? Why does my mother look so afraid? Why don't you want me asking? What happens to a town that stops asking why?"

And the Doubt-Eater's satisfied sound faltered, just slightly, because each question Ivo asked seemed to sting it, like light stinging a thing that lives in the dark.

"Stop that," it hissed. "Stop asking."

And Ivo understood, in a flash of the very insight the creature fed on: her questions hurt it. Of course they did. It ate doubt, it grew fat on the absence of questions — so an actual question, asked right into its face, was the one thing it couldn't stomach. The town had made itself the creature's feast by agreeing to stop asking. But Ivo had never agreed. Ivo couldn't stop. And that made her, to the Doubt-Eater, not food, but poison.

chapters.title: The Question It Couldn't Eat
chapters.body:
The Doubt-Eater rose up out of the well then, furious, a great pale shape of turning pages and cold mist, looming over the small girl who would not stop asking.

"You are a danger," it said, its dry voice gone sharp. "You ask and ask and ask. If the others hear you — if they remember how — they will start asking too. And a town that asks is a town that cannot feed me. I have eaten well for a hundred years. I will not be starved by one small girl." The mist reached for her, cold and smothering. "So I will do to you what I do to their doubts. I will eat your questions. Every one. And you will go smooth and calm and certain like the rest, and never ask why again."

The cold mist wound around Ivo, and she felt it begin to pull at her thoughts, at the endless bubbling stream of why that was the truest part of her — felt it start to draw the questions out, to leave her empty and calm and certain. And it was, for a moment, almost peaceful. To stop asking. To stop wondering. To rest in the smooth still certainty the whole town lived in. Some frightened part of her wanted to let it happen, to finally be like everyone else, to stop being the problem.

But Ivo understood, even as the mist pulled at her, why the creature was so afraid of her — and why the town's peace was not peace at all, but a slow surrender. A person without questions isn't calm. They're asleep. A town that stops asking why stops being able to see when something is wrong — stops being able to change, to grow, to fix its mistakes, to open its north gate and let the world in. The Doubt-Eater didn't give the town peace. It gave them blindness, and called it peace, and ate them hollow a doubt at a time. The questions the town feared weren't a sickness. They were the last living thing about it.

So Ivo did the one thing the creature could not survive. She asked.

Not quietly. Not down into the well. She turned from the mist and threw back her head and shouted her questions up into the sleeping streets of Certain, as loud as her small voice could carry — every why she had, all at once, a flood of them ringing out into the dark: "Why do we never open the north gate? Why do we feed our doubts to a thing in a well? Why are we so afraid to wonder? Why do we call it peace when really we're just asleep? WHY? WHY? WHY?"

And the questions rang through the town like the fire-bell of another story — and the people of Certain woke.

They came to their windows, and their doors, glassy-eyed at first, smooth and calm. But Ivo kept shouting her questions, and a question, once truly heard, is the hardest thing in the world to un-hear. It catches. It spreads. One old woman, at her window, frowned — and thought, for the first time in decades, why do we do this? — and the thought was a question, and it stung the Doubt-Eater like a coal. Then a man wondered it too. Then a child. All across Certain, in the dark, people began, hesitantly, terrifyingly, wonderfully, to ask why — and every question was poison to the thing in the well.

The Doubt-Eater shrieked, a sound of dry pages burning. It had grown fat on a town that didn't ask — and now the whole town was asking at once, a hundred whys ringing out into the night, and it could not eat a fraction of them, and each one seared it. The pale shape thrashed and shrank and thrashed again, starving in the middle of what had been an endless feast, and at last it fled — poured back down into its well, smaller and thinner than it had been in a hundred years, and did not come back up.

Certain was not the same after that night. It was, at first, a far less comfortable place. People asked questions now, and questions lead to arguments, and doubts, and sleepless nights, and all the troublesome unsmooth things the town had traded away long ago. They opened the north gate, and found the world, and had to figure out what to do about it. They wondered if they were doing things right, and sometimes found they weren't, and had to change. It was harder than the smooth certain calm had been. It was so much harder.

But it was awake. It was alive. And when the people of Certain lay awake at night now, turning a question over and over, they no longer wished they could feed it to the well. They understood, at last, what Ivo had known all along: that a question is not a sickness to be cured. It is the sound a mind makes when it is truly alive. And a town — or a person — that has stopped asking why has not found peace. It has only fallen asleep, and called the sleeping peace, and let something in the dark grow fat on the difference.

They renamed the town, in time. They did not call it Certain anymore. They called it Wonder. And Ivo, the girl who could not stop asking, grew up to be its most honored citizen — not because she'd had the answers, but because she'd never stopped asking the questions, even when the whole world wanted her to be quiet.
